why: C spells out what 'Grill Qn', 'plan review round n' and 'Dn' refer to, which a reader outside the conversation needs for the references throughout the spec.
A splits the two complaints (SearXNG dependency, weak results) into labelled bullets so the reader sees the structure at once; B runs them together in one dense paragraph.

B and D name the subject of each sentence (e.g. Consent-O-Matic's zip, Consent-O-Matic's choices, why each engine needs its own profile), where A leaves 'Its choices' and 'the pinned Chromium release zip' ambiguous in a very dense list.
A writes the thresholds out in words (p50 latency is at most 5 s), while C leans on bare symbols and fragments.
C makes the last bullet a full sentence with a subject (web-mcp uses stealth plugins...); the others are otherwise the same.
B and D say the installer does the denying and use a plain active voice; A leaves the actor out.
D's 'Thresholds Q1-Q3 as proposed are fixed' reads awkwardly; A's parallel sentences are clearest.
A calls query, papers and max_passages 'parameters', and so makes clear what is kept; D is the most clipped.
B's 'Every engine uses a fixed English locale' states the rule in one clear sentence; C's opening fragment has no subject.
C is in full sentences with explicit subjects (web-mcp pulls, the installer uses); B is telegraphic and D's 'Installer:' lead-in is clipped.
